summary: Two defects in Nora's conversation memory, both live. One made her quietly stop keeping a running sense of a conversation and fall back to summarising only the last few messages — while the measurement said the opposite. The other let a turn hold a room's queue far longer than the declared limit, and then declared a limit that was not true.
details: The rebuild trigger latched on. After one turn judged unsupported, every later turn rebuilt from scratch rather than building on what came before, because the check looked at the most recent judgement of any age instead of asking whether one had been acted on. Judgements are only recorded for turns that fully succeed, so a single one could hold the trigger open indefinitely.

The counter meant to reveal that failure reported it as healthy, which is why it went unnoticed — the reading a person would use to check was the reading that was wrong. There are now two counters: one for the rebuild being triggered and one for it completing, because a rebuild that keeps failing and a trigger stuck on look identical on either alone.

The fix is a record plus a narrowed read, not a comparison. Two timestamp comparisons were tried first and both were wrong — the second silently DISCARDED a judgement for good if the database was briefly unreadable on the following turn. The conversation's record now names the judgement a rebuild acted on, and the lookup asks only for unsupported judgements: a later successful turn would otherwise bury an older one nobody had acted on, which is the ordinary shape of a good turn after a bad one.

The declared limit on how long a turn may hold a room's queue counted two database calls when there are five, and included a timeout that does not apply to this work at all — so it advertised 165 seconds where the real bound is 45. The count now lives in one place, and a test reads the code's own structure to find every database call, failing if one is added without the limit following or is left with no timeout around it.
limitations: The published ceiling stays at its old, generous value for one deployment. The file that carries it is read at startup while the check that validates it ships in the image, so tightening it in the same change would leave a window where the two disagree and the service refuses to start. It is tightened once the new image is confirmed running.
